title: Nilekani: Tokenisation's Time Has Come — And India Needs Public Chains
excerpt: At the Global Fintech Fest 2026, the Aadhaar architect argued that land, gold and corporate bonds should move to tokenised rails on public blockchains — paired with AI agents that shop for credit 24/7.
body:
• "Now it's very clear that tokenisation, the time has arrived," Nandan Nilekani declared at the Global Fintech Fest 2026, pointing to the RBI's gold-tokenisation review, Maharashtra's plan for a land-tokenisation law, and the SEBI–RBI push on Demat 2.0 and India's first tokenised corporate bond.
  • He defines a token as an asset bundled with all its attributes in one portable package — "a token is an asset with the rules that are traveling with it" — and says today's roughly $600 billion in tokens could swell to an estimated $19 trillion of tokenised assets within seven to eight years.
  • His three India examples: a Tamil Nadu dairy farmer unlocking a Rs 50,000 loan against tokenised cattle, farmers gaining bargaining power through tokenised warehouse receipts, and interoperable loan documents enabling securitisation.
  • For regulated assets, he argues, tokenisation must happen on public chains — private chains can't deliver the liquidity a real market needs — paired with AI agents that can shop tokens to lenders around the clock.

"Now it's very clear that tokenisation, the time has arrived." That was Nandan Nilekani's verdict at the Global Fintech Fest (GFF 2026), where the Aadhaar architect laid out why he believes India should move fast on putting real-world assets on digital rails.

The timing is no accident: the RBI is considering gold tokenisation. Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis has announced a law to tokenise land. And SEBI and the RBI are set to launch Demat 2.0 alongside "India's First Tokenized Corporate Bond." "Companies are already launching these bonds," Nilekani said. "So, clearly there's a lot of action in the era of tokenisation."

What a token actually is

Nilekani explained asset tokenisation in characteristically plain terms: A token, he explained, is an asset "described" with all its attributes, "all bundled together" into one portable package — "portable to give to somebody else."

His analogies were Indian: a government file is a token, he said — documents travelling together from desk to desk. So is a 500-rupee note: "it has everything about the note in the note — its value, its number, the fact that it's certified by the RBI — so whoever receives it is confident they got the full value."

Three examples from the ground

Cattle as collateral. In Udhangarai, Tamil Nadu, a dairy farmer named Devanai leads a cooperative but can't get financing — a distant lender can't verify the animal, confirm ownership or assess its earning potential. In Nilekani's tokenised version, a field officer records each animal's muzzle pattern — "much like a biometric marker" — and issues a verifiable cattle credential covering identity, ownership, age, health and milk productivity. With her consent, the data moves to lenders she chooses; one approved a Rs 50,000 purpose-based loan, spendable at suppliers via QR code.

Warehouse receipts as bargaining power. "If you can unlock warehouse receipts and tokenise them, and then offer that token to multiple lenders, then suddenly you have created liquidity for your inventory," he said. Tokenised, the farmer, the grain, the warehouse and the insurance sit in one portable receipt acceptable to every lender — shifting the bargaining power to the farmer.

Loan documents that travel. "UB and Homewell are now looking at securitising the loans" on marketplaces using standardised, interoperable tokens — "smart contracts to standardise things," creating portability and securitisation.

"A token is an asset with the rules that are traveling with it. And this is designed for interoperability so any bank can use it or any plugin can use it."

— Nandan Nilekani

Why it has to be public chains — and why agents matter

Nilekani's sharpest technical point concerned where tokenisation should live. "If you want to take regulated assets, bonds, and certificates of deposit... how do you get liquidity? That is why you need a public chain. If you do this on a private chain, nobody else has access to the private chain." Public chains bring data-security worries, he conceded — "what you write on the public chain has to be unique but encrypted" — but designing for that is the work regulators must do now.

And he paired tokens with a second force: AI agents. "The agent can package the token and offer it to different kinds of lenders and get loans... Agents that are working 24/7. They are finding markets." A small business, he said, could soon have "a token that proves itself, and a marketplace where we can either sell it or give a loan against it."

What's next

Nilekani said Indian regulators have been invited to a five-day Tech Week at Cambridge's Center for Regulation and Innovation to discuss regulating asset tokenisation. With the RBI, SEBI and state governments all moving in parallel, the question is no longer whether India tokenises real-world assets — it's who sets the rules.
image_caption: Nandan Nilekani speaks at a World Economic Forum session. The Infosys co-founder argues tokenisation's time has come and India needs public blockchains for the next wave of digital assets.
